idiom_name: context object + one state value per state + explicit transition step
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep a context that owns the data all states need plus one reference to the current state; give the state abstraction exactly those operations whose behaviour varies, so no concrete state inherits methods it cannot sensibly implement; let a state perform a transition by asking the context to replace the current state, or let the context map (state, event) pairs to a successor. Decide explicitly whether transitions are owned by the states (this is what distinguishes State from Strategy, but it couples states to their successors) or by a context/transition table (states stay independent at the cost of one indirection). Persist the current state as a stable token, not as a state object or class name, and keep the mapping in code or configuration. For modern tool support, consider XState v5 (actor-model integration, hierarchical/parallel states, guards), python-statemachine (data-driven table form), or source-generated zero-allocation dispatch (Roslyn/C# Source Generators, Rust derive crates) when hot-path performance matters.
pitfalls: Putting state-independent operations on the state interface, forcing every state to implement methods that never vary.
Letting the context test the state type or read state fields instead of delegating, which brings the conditionals back.
Sharing stateless state instances while storing per-context data in them.

State explosion: without hierarchical or orthogonal decomposition, a large flat state space produces O(n²) transitions; start with a table or statechart tool before the number of concrete state classes becomes unmanageable.

Tight inter-state coupling: when each concrete state directly instantiates its successor(s), the entire graph must be updated whenever a new state is inserted; avoid new-ing states inside other states and prefer a context-scoped factory or transition table.

Broken encapsulation: passing the entire context (or a large interface) to every state leaks internals and makes states fragile to context changes; pass only the minimal slice each state actually needs.

Forgetting the default/fallback state: every state machine needs a handler for unexpected events (ignore, log-and-reject, or recover); omitting this makes the machine silently swallow events in unhandled combinations.

Storing mutable per-context data in shared stateless state instances: even if the state object appears stateless, any field written during handling becomes shared mutable state across all contexts holding that instance.

Allocations on hot paths: heap allocation per transition (e.g., make_unique in C++ GoF pattern) adds ~10–12 ns per transition; for high-frequency events, prefer enum + switch (zero allocations, ~0.7 ns/mission) or source-generated dispatch (ZeroAlloc.StateMachine achieves ~36 ns vs ~4,495 ns for library-based dispatch).

Missing serialisation safeguards: persisting state objects or class references directly; refactoring a class name breaks stored data; always persist a stable token (enum, string ID) and map to state instances on deserialisation.

Ignoring concurrency: non-atomic read-modify-write on the state reference permits race conditions; use AtomicReference (JVM), Compare-And-Swap (CAS), or a single-threaded owner to serialise transitions.
Bypassing the transition method: letting callers write ctx.state = X directly destroys transition validation; make the state field private and route every change through a single transition method.

Wrong move: modelling every in-flight external call as its own transient state (waitingForPayment, waitingForShippingA, waitingForShippingB, ...) so async replies have somewhere to land -> the state space multiplies by the number of pending calls and late or out-of-order replies drive the machine into states that were never entered -> instead keep one state, correlate replies against a request identifier stored as context data, and queue or postpone events the current state cannot handle (Erlang gen_statem postpone_action re-delivers postponed events only after an actual state change) so stale replies are discarded, not misrouted.
